title: 10.2 Small Group · Group 1
contentObjective: With my small group, I can use bilateral symmetry to describe structure in nature and in human creations — one step at a time, with support.
languageObjective: I can talk through each step out loud using a sentence frame and the lesson's key words.

noticeAndWonder.context: A butterfly rests on a leaf with its wings spread wide open. The pattern of spots and colors on the left wing repeats on the right wing.
noticeStarters: I notice the pattern of spots ___ .
I notice down the middle of the butterfly ___ .
wonderStarters: I wonder why people find butterflies ___ .

turnAndTalk.question: The butterfly's two wings are mirror images across a line down the middle of its body. Why does drawing that line matter for proving the butterfly is symmetric?
turnAndTalk.kernel: A figure is symmetric only if there is a specific line where one side is a mirror image of the other.

stems.en: Drawing the line matters because it lets us ___ the two sides.
stems.es: Trazar la línea importa porque nos permite ___ los dos lados.

stems.en: The butterfly is symmetric because its two sides are ___ of each other.
stems.es: La mariposa es simétrica porque sus dos lados son ___ el uno del otro.

turnAndTalk.extend: Could a butterfly still be symmetric if its line of symmetry ran at an angle instead of straight down the middle? Justify your answer.
extendStems: Yes/No, because a line of symmetry ___.
The direction of the line ___ whether the figure is symmetric.

turnAndTalk.question: When you sorted cards into 'has bilateral symmetry' and 'no bilateral symmetry,' why did the letter R end up in the 'no' column while a ladybug seen from above ended up in the 'yes' column?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The test is whether some line divides the figure into two mirror-image halves; the letter R fails that test, but a ladybug's left and right sides match.

stems.en: The letter R has no bilateral symmetry because ___.
stems.es: La letra R no tiene simetría bilateral porque ___.

stems.en: The ladybug has bilateral symmetry because ___.
stems.es: La mariquita tiene simetría bilateral porque ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: The spiral snail shell was sorted into 'no bilateral symmetry.' Could you argue it has a DIFFERENT kind of symmetry? What would you call it?
extendStems: The snail shell does not have bilateral symmetry, but it might have ___ symmetry because ___.
This is different from bilateral symmetry because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: A plant grows in layers, with 2 mirror-image leaves per layer. After 4 layers, how many leaves are there, and how does that connect to bilateral symmetry?
turnAndTalk.kernel: 4 layers × 2 leaves per layer = 8 leaves, and each layer's 2 leaves are a mirror-image pair.

stems.en: After 4 layers, the plant has ___ leaves because ___.
stems.es: Después de 4 capas, la planta tiene ___ hojas porque ___.

stems.en: Each layer shows bilateral symmetry because ___.
stems.es: Cada capa muestra simetría bilateral porque ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: If a plant grew 6 layers instead of 4, how many leaves would it have, and would each layer still show bilateral symmetry? Explain.
extendStems: With 6 layers, the plant would have ___ leaves because ___.
Each layer would still/would not show bilateral symmetry because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice, when you had to decide if a figure had bilateral symmetry, what strategy helped you check it — even when the line of symmetry wasn't vertical?
turnAndTalk.kernel: A figure has bilateral symmetry if ANY line — not just a vertical one — makes the two sides mirror images.

stems.en: I checked by ___ to see if the two sides were ___.
stems.es: Comprobé al ___ para ver si los dos lados eran ___.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who assumed a line of symmetry always has to be vertical? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ first because ___.
The mistake happens when you ___ instead of ___.

vocabulary.definition: Having two halves that match — one side is a mirror image of the other.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Que tiene dos mitades que coinciden: un lado es la imagen reflejada del otro.
vocabulary.example: The two sides of the butterfly look like mirror images. The butterfly is symmetric.

vocabulary.definition: A copy of a shape flipped across a line, like a reflection in a mirror.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una copia de una figura volteada sobre una línea, como un reflejo en un espejo.
vocabulary.example: The left wing of a butterfly is a mirror image of the right wing.

vocabulary.definition: Reflective symmetry in plants and animals — the two sides of the body mirror each other.
vocabulary.definitionEs: La simetría reflectiva en plantas y animales: los dos lados del cuerpo se reflejan entre sí.
vocabulary.example: All butterflies have reflective symmetry; in plants and animals this is called bilateral symmetry.

vocabulary.definition: The line you can draw through a figure so each side is a reflection of the other.
vocabulary.definitionEs: La línea que puedes trazar por una figura de modo que cada lado sea el reflejo del otro.
vocabulary.example: We can draw a line down the middle of the layer of leaves, along the center of each leaf.

vocabulary.definition: An even, steady arrangement — neither side feels heavier than the other.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una disposición pareja y estable: ningún lado se siente más pesado que el otro.
vocabulary.example: Our brains are wired to favor balance, and bilateral symmetry provides balance.

launch.narrative: This is your support small group for Lesson 10.2. We're going to slow this down and build it together, one step at a time. You can ask a question any time — that's what this group is for.

conceptIntro.heading: Let's build it together — Math creates beautiful designs in nature
conceptIntro.intro: Look closely at a butterfly's wings, then at how a plant grows its leaves. The same mathematical idea keeps appearing. We'll walk through a worked example, try one together, then you'll try a few with hints right there when you need them.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Bilateral symmetry — two sides that are mirror images — appears throughout nature, and it shapes human creations from art to music to architecture.

iDo.title: Watch me find the symmetry in a butterfly
lines: I look at the two sides of the butterfly, and they look like mirror images — the butterfly is symmetric.
All butterflies have reflective symmetry. In plants and animals, this is called bilateral symmetry.
To show it, I draw a line down the middle of the butterfly's body: everything on the left is reflected on the right.

weDo.title: Let's find the symmetry in a growing plant
lines: This plant grows in layers, and each layer is made up of two leaves — so 3 layers hold 3 × 2 = 6 leaves.
In the first layer, one leaf is a mirror image of the other.
To show the bilateral symmetry in the second layer, we draw a line down the middle of the layer, along the center of each leaf.
Are the leaves EXACTLY symmetric? Nature comes close, but living things are never perfectly identical.
Sentence frame — say it with me: "The multiples/steps I need are ___ , and the answer is ___ ."

youDo.title: Now you try — with support
lines: Try the practice problems below. The hint button is right there whenever you get stuck — use it, that's smart.
Remember the key idea: Bilateral symmetry — two sides that are mirror images — appears throughout nature, and it shapes human creations from art to music to architecture..

explore.label: Does it have bilateral symmetry? Sort each one.

cards.text: A butterfly with wings spread open
A human face seen from the front
A layer of two leaves that are mirror images

explore.instructions: Quick warm-up together: Test each one the same way: imagine drawing a line down the middle. If one side is a mirror image of the other, it has bilateral symmetry. After sorting, name where the line of symmetry runs on one card from the left column.

diagram.title: Bilateral Symmetry on a Grid
diagram.caption: Plot each point, right then up; the line x = 6 acts as the line of symmetry, so every point at x = 4 has a mirror partner at x = 8 the same distance away and the two halves match.

connect.scenario: Your friend insists that only one of two flowers has bilateral symmetry. One flower's petals mirror each other across a line down its center; the other flower does too, just along a different line.
connect.promptQuestion: How do you respond to your friend?
connect.prompt: To settle the disagreement, draw a ___ through the center of each flower and check whether one side is a ___ of the other. If the test works for both, then ___ flowers have bilateral symmetry.

check.stem: A butterfly's two wings look like mirror images of each other across a line down the center of its body. What is this type of symmetry called?
choices: Rotational symmetry
Bilateral symmetry
Radial symmetry
Point symmetry
check.explanation: Bilateral symmetry means one line divides a shape into two mirror-image halves, like the butterfly's wings. Rotational and radial symmetry involve a shape repeating around a center point, and point symmetry involves matching after a 180° turn — neither describes a single mirror line.

check.stem: To test whether a flower has bilateral symmetry, what should you do first?
choices: Count the number of petals
Measure the flower's height
Draw a line through the center and compare the two sides
Compare the flower to a different type of flower
check.explanation: Bilateral symmetry is tested by drawing a line through the center and checking whether the two sides are mirror images. Counting petals or measuring height doesn't test whether the halves match, and comparing to a different flower doesn't test this flower's own symmetry.

check.stem: Your friend says only one of two flowers has bilateral symmetry. You test both by drawing a line through each flower's center and find both sides match on both flowers. What is most likely true?
choices: The friend is right — only one flower truly has symmetry
Both flowers have bilateral symmetry, but the second flower's line of symmetry likely runs in a direction the friend didn't try
Symmetry cannot be tested in flowers
The two flowers must be identical in shape to both be symmetric
check.explanation: Since the test showed both flowers have a line where the sides mirror each other, both are bilaterally symmetric — the friend likely only checked one direction on the second flower and missed its line of symmetry. Flowers don't need to look alike to each have their own symmetry.

connect.modelAnswer: I would tell my friend we should test both flowers the same way instead of just looking quickly. For each flower, I would draw a line through its center and check whether one side is a mirror image of the other. If both flowers pass the test, then both have bilateral symmetry — the second flower's line of symmetry might just run in a direction my friend did not try.

diagram.title: Mirror distances from the line of symmetry
diagram.caption: Both wings sit 2 units from 6, so the halves match — that equal distance is what bilateral symmetry means

approaching.stem: What does it mean that a butterfly is symmetric?
choices: The two sides of the butterfly look like mirror images
The butterfly has exactly two wings
The butterfly's wings are very colorful
The butterfly is larger than most insects
approaching.explanation: Symmetric means one side is a mirror image of the other — that is exactly what we see across the butterfly's body.
choiceFeedback: Having two wings is not enough — the two sides must MIRROR each other to be symmetric.
Color makes a butterfly pretty, but symmetry is about the two sides matching, not about color.
Size has nothing to do with symmetry — a tiny butterfly is just as symmetric as a big one.
hints: Think about what you see on the left wing versus the right wing.
Imagine a mirror standing along the butterfly's body.
What word describes two sides that reflect each other?

approaching.stem: In plants and animals, reflective symmetry is called:
choices: bilateral symmetry
rotational symmetry
a mirror image
balance
approaching.explanation: The lesson says it directly: all butterflies have reflective symmetry, and in plants and animals this is called bilateral symmetry.
choiceFeedback: Rotational symmetry is about turning a shape, not reflecting it across a line.
A mirror image is what each SIDE is — the name for the whole property in living things is different.
Balance is why our brains find symmetry pleasing, not the name of the symmetry itself.
hints: The word starts with 'bi-', meaning two.
It describes the two sides of a body.
Bi-lateral means two-sided.

approaching.stem: A plant grows in layers, and each layer is made up of 2 leaves. How many leaves does the plant have after growing 4 layers?
choices: 8 leaves
6 leaves
16 leaves
4 leaves
choiceFeedback: 6 comes from adding 4 + 2 instead of multiplying.
16 doubles the layers first (4 × 2 = 8, then × 2 again) — each layer has 2 leaves, not 4.
4 counts the layers but forgets each layer holds 2 leaves.
hints: How many leaves are in ONE layer?
There are 4 equal layers.
Multiply 4 × 2.

approaching.stem: Where have you seen symmetry before? Name one place and describe it.
approaching.modelAnswer: I have seen symmetry in my own face in the mirror — my left side and right side are almost mirror images of each other, with an eye and an ear on each side.

approaching.stem: How can you SHOW that a layer of two leaves has bilateral symmetry?
choices: Draw a line down the middle of the layer and check that each side mirrors the other
Count the total number of leaves on the plant
Measure how tall the plant is
Color the two leaves different colors
approaching.explanation: The lesson's method: draw a line down the middle of the layer, along the center of each leaf, and see that one side is a mirror image of the other.
choiceFeedback: Counting leaves tells you how many there are, not whether the two sides mirror each other.
Height says nothing about whether the left side reflects the right side.
Coloring them differently would actually BREAK the mirror-image match, not demonstrate it.
hints: Symmetry is about two sides matching.
You need something for the sides to reflect ACROSS.
What did we draw down the middle of the butterfly?

approaching.stem: Name one animal besides a butterfly that has bilateral symmetry.
approaching.modelAnswer: A dragonfly has bilateral symmetry — its left wings and right wings are mirror images across the line of its body.

onLevel.stem: Why do people find symmetry pleasing?
choices: Our brains are wired to favor balance, and bilateral symmetry provides balance
Symmetric things are always brightly colored
Symmetry only appears in rare and expensive objects
Symmetric shapes are always larger than non-symmetric ones
onLevel.explanation: The lesson says it directly: our brains are wired to favor balance, and bilateral symmetry provides balance.
choiceFeedback: Color is separate from symmetry — a plain gray moth can be perfectly symmetric.
Symmetry is everywhere in nature, from leaves to ladybugs — it is common, not rare.
Size has nothing to do with it — a tiny symmetric leaf is as balanced as a huge one.
hints: The answer is about how our brains respond.
What does bilateral symmetry provide that brains favor?
Think of an even, steady arrangement.

onLevel.stem: There are over 17,000 species of butterflies, and ALL butterflies have reflective symmetry. About how many of those species have reflective symmetry?
choices: All 17,000+ of them
About half of them
Only the most colorful ones
None — symmetry is only in plants
onLevel.explanation: 'All butterflies have reflective symmetry' means every one of the 17,000+ species — no exceptions.
choiceFeedback: 'All' means every single species, not half of them.
Symmetry is about the two sides matching, not about how colorful the wings are.
The butterfly itself was our first example — animals show bilateral symmetry too.
hints: Read the statement carefully: ALL butterflies.
Does 'all' leave any out?
Every species means every species.

onLevel.stem: Are the two leaves in a real plant layer EXACTLY symmetric? Why might this be?
onLevel.modelAnswer: No — the leaves are close to mirror images but not exact. Real plants grow in messy conditions: one leaf might get more sun or get nibbled by an insect, so the two sides come out slightly different. Nature follows the pattern of bilateral symmetry without being perfect.

onLevel.stem: A plant grows 2 leaves at a time, one layer per week. How many leaves has it grown after 6 weeks?
choices: 12 leaves
8 leaves
6 leaves
36 leaves
onLevel.explanation: One layer per week for 6 weeks is 6 layers, and 6 layers × 2 leaves = 12 leaves.
choiceFeedback: 8 comes from adding 6 + 2 instead of multiplying.
6 counts the layers but forgets each layer holds 2 leaves.
36 squares the 6 weeks (6 × 6) instead of multiplying weeks by leaves per layer.
hints: How many layers grow in 6 weeks?
Each layer is made up of 2 leaves.
Multiply 6 × 2.

onLevel.stem: Where else do you see bilateral symmetry — in nature OR in something humans made?
onLevel.modelAnswer: I see bilateral symmetry in the front of my school building: the doors are in the center, and the windows on the left side mirror the windows on the right side. The line of symmetry runs straight down through the middle of the doors.

onLevel.stem: Which is the best test for whether a figure has bilateral symmetry?
choices: Find a line where one side is the mirror image of the other
Check whether the figure has an even number of parts
Check whether the figure is found in nature
Check whether the figure looks beautiful to you
onLevel.explanation: Bilateral symmetry means exactly this: there is a line across which the two sides are mirror images.
choiceFeedback: An even number of parts is not enough — the letter Z has 2 matching ends but no mirror line.
Humans create bilateral symmetry too, in art, music, and architecture — nature is not required.
Beauty is an opinion; the mirror-image test gives the same answer no matter who runs it.
hints: Go back to the definition, not the feeling.
What must exist for the two sides to reflect across?
Mirror image across a line.

practice.commonMistake: Thinking a figure lacks bilateral symmetry just because its line of symmetry is not vertical — the mirror line can run in any direction, and the test is whether the two sides match across it.

exitTicket.stem: Quick check — you've got this: Which statement best shows what this lesson means by 'math is beauty'?
choices: Math creates beautiful designs like bilateral symmetry, found in nature and used in human art, music, and architecture
Only things made by mathematicians can be beautiful
Butterflies are the only living things with symmetry
Beauty and math are opposites — one is feeling and one is numbers
exitTicket.explanation: The summary makes the claim in two parts: bilateral symmetry appears naturally in many plants and animals, and it also influences human creations from art to music to architecture.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It mentions nature AND human creations.
Which option includes both?
